title: SHOULD CHRISTIANS OBSERVE LENT? THE UNCOMFORTABLE TRUTH ABOUT A TRADITION JESUS NEVER COMMANDED
paragraphs: SHOULD CHRISTIANS OBSERVE LENT? THE UNCOMFORTABLE TRUTH ABOUT A TRADITION JESUS NEVER COMMANDED

Forty days of fasting. Ashes on foreheads. Sacrifices made in God's name. But what if the greatest danger isn't observing Lent—or refusing to observe it—but missing the very Savior it is supposed to honor?
Imagine standing before Jesus Christ and telling Him everything you gave up for Lent.
The coffee you stopped drinking.
The meat you refused to eat.
The social media accounts you temporarily abandoned.
The sweets you pushed away, the meals you skipped, the religious services you attended.
And then imagine hearing a question that reaches far deeper than your sacrifices.
"But did you give Me your heart?"
That question should disturb us.
Not because fasting is wrong. Not because Lent is necessarily sinful. And certainly not because every Christian who observes Lent is merely performing empty religious rituals.
But because there is something frightening about the possibility of doing religious things for the right God while allowing our hearts to remain far from Him.
A person can spend forty days abstaining from chocolate while continuing to feed bitterness.
Someone can walk into church with ashes on their forehead while carrying unforgiveness they refuse to surrender.
A believer can faithfully observe a religious season while neglecting prayer, repentance, mercy, and obedience throughout the rest of the year.
And someone who proudly refuses to observe Lent can be just as spiritually blind, mistaking contempt for tradition as proof of biblical faithfulness.
That is where this conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Because the real question isn't simply whether Lent is biblical.
The deeper question is whether our religious practices are leading us closer to Jesus—or quietly replacing the surrender He actually requires.
And before you decide which side of this debate you're on, there is something in Scripture you need to see.
Something about forty days.
Something about fasting.
Something about human traditions.
And something about the difference between remembering the cross and actually following the One who died upon it.
Because this isn't merely a debate about a religious calendar.
It is a question about the condition of the human heart.
And that includes yours.
The word Lent comes through Old English lencten, associated with springtime. It is not a biblical Hebrew or Greek term, nor does the word itself appear in the original text of Scripture.

Lent developed within the history of the Christian Church as a season of preparation before Easter, commonly emphasizing prayer, fasting, repentance, generosity, and reflection on Christ's suffering, death, and resurrection.

In many Western Christian traditions, Lent begins on Ash Wednesday and extends toward Easter, with forty fasting days traditionally counted by excluding Sundays. Eastern Christian traditions have related but distinct fasting calendars and practices.

Its historical development was gradual. Early Christians practiced fasting in preparation for Easter, but the duration and form varied. By the fourth century, a forty-day preparation was becoming well established in various Christian communities.
That distinction matters.
Lent is an ecclesiastical tradition, not a forty-day observance directly commanded by Jesus or the apostles.
But does that automatically make it wrong?
Not necessarily.
And does its widespread acceptance automatically make it right?
Absolutely not.
Scripture—not popularity, antiquity, denominational loyalty, or personal preference—must guide our evaluation.
Consider what happened immediately after Jesus was baptized.
Matthew 4:1–2 records that the Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness, where He fasted for forty days and forty nights before facing temptation.
The Greek text of Matthew 4:2 says:
καὶ νηστεύσας ἡμέρας τεσσεράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσεράκοντα, ὕστερον ἐπείνασεν.
Kaì nēsteúsas hēméras tesserákonta kaì nýktas tesserákonta, hýsteron epeínasen.
A faithful translation is:
"And having fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward He was hungry."
The Greek participle νηστεύσας (nēsteúsas) comes from nēsteuō, meaning "to fast" or "to abstain from food."
Jesus truly fasted.
His hunger was real.
His physical weakness was real.
And the temptation that followed was real.
But notice what Matthew does not say.
Matthew does not command every Christian to repeat Jesus' forty-day fast annually.
Matthew does not establish Lent.
Matthew does not instruct the Church to mark its members with ashes or to observe a particular pre-Easter calendar.
The passage describes a decisive event in the earthly ministry of Jesus Christ.
And its meaning reaches far beyond an example of personal discipline.
Where Israel had failed during its wilderness testing, Jesus remained faithful.
Where humanity repeatedly surrendered to temptation, Christ obeyed.
When Satan tempted Him to turn stones into bread, Jesus answered with Scripture.
Matthew 4:4 records His response:
"Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God." (KJV)
Jesus was quoting Deuteronomy 8:3.
The Hebrew expression at the heart of that passage is:
כִּי עַל־כָּל־מוֹצָא פִי־יְהוָה יִחְיֶה הָאָדָם
Ki al-kol motza fi-YHWH yichyeh ha-adam.
Meaning:
"But by everything that comes from the mouth of the LORD shall man live."
The message is not that food is evil.
It is that human beings depend ultimately upon God.
And here is the beautiful truth that must never be lost in our discussion of Lent:
Jesus did not fast forty days to establish a religious competition. He stood faithful where sinners had failed, fulfilling His mission as the obedient Son.
His wilderness victory points toward the greater victory He would accomplish through His death and resurrection.
We are not saved because we successfully imitate forty days of fasting.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that unmistakably clear.
And this is where some Christians become deeply concerned about Lent.
They remember the warning Jesus gave about human traditions.
In Mark 7:8, Jesus declared:
"For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men..." (KJV)
The Greek text begins:
ἀφέντες τὴν ἐντολὴν τοῦ θεοῦ κρατεῖτε τὴν παράδοσιν τῶν ἀνθρώπων
Aphéntes tēn entolēn tou Theou krateîte tēn parádosin tōn anthrōpōn.
In context, Jesus was confronting religious leaders who elevated certain inherited practices in ways that undermined God's commandments.
The Greek word παράδοσις (parádosis) means "tradition" or "that which is handed down."
But we must be careful.
The word itself is not automatically negative.
In 2 Thessalonians 2:15, Paul tells believers to hold firmly to the traditions they had been taught through apostolic teaching, whether spoken or written.
Therefore, the biblical issue is not simply whether something is called a tradition.
The issue is its source, content, authority, and relationship to God's revealed will.
A tradition becomes spiritually dangerous when it contradicts Scripture, displaces God's commandments, claims authority God has not given it, or becomes a false measure of righteousness.
That principle should humble Christians on every side.
Someone who observes Lent must never teach that participation earns forgiveness or makes a person more deserving of salvation.
Someone who does not observe Lent must never assume that every believer who practices it is worshiping God in vain.
And no Christian should turn a disputed calendar observance into a substitute for the Gospel.
Because the cross was not an invitation to build a ladder of religious achievements toward heaven.
It was the place where the sinless Savior gave Himself for sinners who could never climb high enough.
Now consider another passage.
Jesus said in Matthew 6:16:
"Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance..." (KJV)
Notice His wording.
When you fast.
Not simply "if you fast."
Jesus anticipated that fasting would have a place in the spiritual lives of His disciples.
But He immediately confronted the temptation to turn fasting into a public performance.
In Matthew 6:17–18, He instructed His followers to anoint their heads and wash their faces so their fasting would not be displayed for human applause.
This does not mean every publicly known fast is automatically sinful. Scripture also records communal fasts, including the worshiping and fasting of believers in Acts 13:2–3.
The issue is motive.
Who are you trying to impress?
God?
Or the people watching you?
That question reaches into places we would rather leave untouched.
Because sometimes we want others to know how spiritual we are.
We want people to notice the sacrifices.
We want our religious seriousness to become visible.
We want to be recognized as disciplined, devoted, and holy.
But the Father sees what happens when nobody is watching.
He sees the words you type and delete.
He sees how you treat your family after church.
He sees the resentment you keep rehearsing.
He sees the private compromise you have learned to excuse.
He sees whether your fasting is accompanied by love, humility, repentance, and justice.
And He sees the person who quietly prays through tears without ever announcing it online.
God is not impressed by the appearance of surrender when the heart is determined to remain in control.
That truth becomes even sharper in Isaiah 58.
The people of Israel were fasting, yet God confronted their oppression, quarrels, and injustice.
In Isaiah 58:6, God asks:
"Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens..." (KJV)
The Hebrew phrase begins:
הֲלוֹא זֶה צוֹם אֶבְחָרֵהוּ
Halo zeh tzom evcharehu.
Meaning:
"Is not this the fast that I choose?"
The Hebrew word צוֹם (tzom) means "fast."
The passage does not abolish fasting.
It exposes fasting separated from righteousness and compassion.
God was confronting people who practiced religious self-denial while continuing to harm others.
And that warning is painfully relevant today.
What good is giving up meat while feeding cruelty?
What good is avoiding sweets while refusing to forgive?
What good is fasting from entertainment while neglecting your children?
What good is abstaining from food while withholding generosity from someone who is hungry?
What good is observing a season of repentance while refusing to acknowledge the sin you already know God is confronting?
These questions are not arguments against fasting.
They are arguments against hypocrisy.
And they should challenge those who observe Lent and those who never have.
Because we can reject a religious tradition and still cling to the very sins that tradition was intended to confront.
We can defend biblical truth in public while refusing to obey it in private.
We can win arguments about Lent and still lose sight of love.
And perhaps that is the tragedy.
We become so busy debating the practice that we stop examining the person practicing it.
Us.
Our hearts.
Our motives.
Our desperate need for grace.
But there is another passage we must consider if we want to be faithful to the whole counsel of Scripture.
Romans 14.
Paul addresses believers who differed over food and the observance of particular days.
Romans 14:5–6 says:
"One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind. He that regardeth the day, regardeth it unto the Lord..." (KJV)
The Greek expression in Romans 14:5 is:
ἕκαστος ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ νοῒ πληροφορείσθω
Hékastos en tō idíō noḯ plērophoreísthō.
A faithful translation is:
"Let each person be fully convinced in his own mind."
Paul's immediate discussion concerns differences of conscience among believers. He was not specifically discussing Lent, which developed later in Christian history.
Nevertheless, the passage gives an important principle for evaluating disputable observances.
Believers should act with sincere conviction before the Lord rather than condemning one another over matters Scripture has not universally commanded.
This does not mean every religious practice is acceptable.
Paul elsewhere strongly rejects practices that compromise the Gospel or place believers under false spiritual obligations.

Galatians 4:9–11 warns against returning to bondage through religious observances. Colossians 2:16–23 warns against being judged over food and festivals and against self-imposed religion that lacks power to overcome sinful desires.
These passages must be considered together.

The New Testament leaves room for sincere differences over certain days and practices, while firmly rejecting attempts to make human observances necessary for salvation, spiritual superiority, or acceptance before God.
So can a Christian observe Lent with a clear conscience?
Yes, provided the observance does not contradict Scripture, replace obedience, or become a condition of salvation or righteousness before God.
Can a Christian refuse to observe Lent with a clear conscience?
Yes.
Christians are not commanded in the New Testament to keep a forty-day pre-Easter fast.
Observing Lent does not make someone a better Christian. Refusing Lent does not automatically make someone a more biblical Christian. Faithfulness to Jesus is the issue.
And there is something else we should understand.
In Mark 2:19–20, Jesus described Himself as the bridegroom and spoke of a time when His disciples would fast after the bridegroom was taken away.
The passage establishes a place for fasting among His followers.
But it does not establish Lent as a required annual observance.
The Church may organize times for prayer, teaching, fasting, and remembrance, but such practices must remain servants of the Gospel, never its masters.
A church calendar can remind believers of Christ.
It cannot replace Christ.
A season of fasting can help someone devote attention to prayer.
It cannot purchase God's favor.
An ash cross can symbolize human mortality and repentance.
It cannot cleanse a guilty conscience.
Only Jesus saves.
Only His blood atones for sin.
Only His resurrection secures the hope of eternal life.
And that brings us to one of the most moving moments in the entire Bible.
David had committed terrible sins.
Adultery.
Deception.
The orchestration of another man's death.
He was a king with power, influence, and religious knowledge.
Yet none of those things could erase what he had done.
When confronted by the prophet Nathan, David could no longer hide behind his position.
He confessed.
And Psalm 51 gives us a window into his brokenness.
Psalm 51:17 declares:
"The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise." (KJV)
The Hebrew expression is:
לֵב־נִשְׁבָּר וְנִדְכֶּה
Lev-nishbar venidkeh.
"A broken and crushed heart."
The Hebrew words communicate a heart shattered and humbled before God.
David was not suggesting that repentance could be reduced to emotion or that God's commands no longer mattered.
He was acknowledging that religious offerings could not substitute for genuine contrition.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You have attended services.
You have sung worship songs.
You have posted Bible verses.
You have tried to look strong.
But somewhere beneath the religious language is a heart carrying guilt.
Something you did.
Something you said.
Someone you wounded.
A habit you keep returning to.
A secret you are terrified someone will discover.
And perhaps every time you hear a message about repentance, you wonder whether God could still receive someone like you.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not that your sin was insignificant.
The Gospel is that Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
The cross does not minimize sin.
It reveals how serious sin is—and how astonishing God's grace truly is.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
While we were still sinners.
Not after forty days of perfect discipline.
Not after we had finally repaired our reputations.
Not after we had managed to appear holy enough.
While we were sinners.
Christ died for us.
And this is why our Gospel Warrior theme matters so deeply.
Think about the woman caught in adultery in John 8:1–11.
She was brought before Jesus in humiliation.
Her accusers were ready to condemn her.
Her sin was being used as a public spectacle.
Jesus did not pretend that sin was harmless.
Nor did He join the crowd in treating her as though her failure was the end of her story.
He told her:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." (John 8:11, KJV)
Mercy.
And a call to leave sin.
Grace.
And transformation.
That is the beauty of Christ.
He does not offer forgiveness so we can comfortably remain enslaved to the sins destroying us.
He calls us out of darkness and into newness of life.

And although the account of the woman caught in adultery has a well-known textual history—being absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts—the mercy and holiness it portrays are consistent with the broader New Testament witness to Jesus.
Consider Peter.
He denied Jesus three times.
Not once.
Three times.
The man who had declared his loyalty crumbled under pressure.
Then the rooster crowed.
And Peter wept bitterly.
But failure was not the final word over his life.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
Or consider Saul of Tarsus.
A persecutor of the Church.
A man associated with violence against believers.
Yet Christ confronted him, showed him mercy, and transformed his life.
The persecutor became an apostle proclaiming the Savior he once opposed.
Not because his past was imaginary.
Not because his actions were harmless.
But because the risen Jesus is powerful enough to redeem the undeserving.
This is the Gospel.
And this is why Lent, if observed, must point beyond itself.
Beyond ashes.
Beyond fasting schedules.
Beyond religious customs.
Beyond forty days.
Toward the crucified and risen Christ.
Because a religious season cannot rewrite your story.
Jesus can.
Now imagine a different kind of Lent.
Not one where someone gives up a favorite drink simply to prove they can endure forty days without it.

But one where a believer uses the season to confront an addiction, seek accountability, pray faithfully, reconcile with someone they have wronged, care for the poor, and meditate deeply on the suffering and resurrection of Christ.
Would those actions be wrong simply because they occurred during Lent?
Of course not.
Those are good responses to biblical truth, though their value does not depend on the calendar.
Now imagine someone who chooses not to observe Lent.
Instead, that believer practices prayer, fasting, generosity, repentance, and Scripture meditation throughout the year without adopting a particular liturgical season.
Would that believer be disobedient for not participating in Lent?
No.
The New Testament does not impose Lent as a requirement.
The question is not whether every Christian must follow the same devotional calendar.
The question is whether we are walking in obedience to the same Lord.
And here is where the discussion becomes even more personal.
What happens after Lent ends?
What happens when the fasting season is over?
When the foods return?
When the regular routines resume?
When the religious excitement fades?
Does your pursuit of holiness disappear with the calendar?
Does your prayer life go silent?
Does your generosity stop?
Does your repentance become something you postpone until the next religious season?
Because Jesus did not say:
He said:
"If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me." (Luke 9:23, KJV)
Daily.
The Greek word is:
καθ᾽ ἡμέραν
Kath' hēméran.
"Day by day."
That expression appears in Luke's account and emphasizes the ongoing nature of discipleship.
Following Christ is not a seasonal performance.
It is a lifelong response to grace.
Not a means of earning salvation, but the fruit of belonging to the Savior.
And perhaps this is the truth we have been avoiding.
We are often willing to give up something temporarily.
But surrendering ourselves completely?
That is harder.
Giving up sugar for forty days may be uncomfortable.
Giving up the pride that keeps destroying your relationships may be agonizing.
Skipping a meal can be difficult.
Confessing a hidden sin can feel terrifying.
Turning off social media may require discipline.
Turning away from a cherished idol may require the painful honesty of admitting how much control it has over your heart.
But Christ does not call us merely to temporary inconvenience.
He calls us to repentance and faith.
And He gives grace to those who come to Him.
The Greek word often translated "repentance" is μετάνοια (metánoia), referring to a change of mind or heart that involves turning from sin toward God.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling bad because you were exposed.
It involves acknowledging sin, turning toward God, and seeking to walk in obedience through His grace.
It is not a payment for forgiveness.
It is a proper response to the God who calls sinners to Himself.
And that is why the words of Joel 2:13 are so powerful:
"And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God..." (KJV)
The Hebrew reads:
וְקִרְעוּ לְבַבְכֶם וְאַל־בִּגְדֵיכֶם
Veqir'u levavkhem ve'al-bigdeikhem.
"Rend your hearts, and not your garments."
In ancient Israel, tearing garments could express grief, distress, or repentance.
But God was calling His people beyond the outward sign.
He wanted genuine turning.
Not merely torn clothing.
Torn hearts.
Not merely visible sorrow.
True repentance.
And this is the passage I wish every Christian would remember whenever Lent becomes a source of pride, division, or religious performance.
God is not looking for the most impressive outward display of repentance. He calls for the heart to turn back to Him.
Whether you observe Lent or not, that call remains.
Whether your church practices Ash Wednesday or not, that call remains.
Whether you fast before Easter or at another time, that call remains.
The same Jesus who calls sinners to repentance also promises rest to those who come to Him.
And if you are exhausted from trying to prove yourself worthy of God's love, you need to hear this.
You cannot earn the cross.
You cannot purchase the resurrection.
You cannot make yourself worthy of grace through the number of meals you skip or the number of religious services you attend.
Jesus Christ accomplished what we could never accomplish.
He lived in perfect obedience.
He died for sins.
He rose from the dead.
And He calls us to turn from sin and trust in Him.
This does not make spiritual discipline meaningless.
It gives spiritual discipline its proper place.
We pray because we depend upon God.
We fast to humble ourselves and devote attention to Him.
We give because His generosity transforms our hearts.
We obey because we love the One who first loved us.
We do not do these things to force God to save us.
We do them as people responding to His grace.
And if Lent helps you remember those truths, practice it with humility, biblical discernment, and a clear conscience before God.
If you choose not to observe Lent, do not despise those who sincerely seek Christ through that season.
But if Lent has become a substitute for daily discipleship, you need more than another religious routine.
You need to return to Jesus.
And if rejecting Lent has become a badge of spiritual superiority, you also need to examine your heart.
Because pride can wear ashes.
And pride can also boast about never wearing them.
Both need the same Savior.
Perhaps you have been reading this article while quietly carrying something nobody knows about.
A marriage that is breaking.
A child you desperately want to see return to God.
A faith that feels weaker than it once did.
A secret struggle that has lasted longer than you ever imagined.
A painful memory that still makes you question whether you can be forgiven.
Maybe you have spent years looking religious while privately feeling spiritually empty.
Or perhaps you have avoided church because you assumed Christianity was nothing more than rules, rituals, and people judging one another.
Please do not confuse the failures of religious people with the character of Jesus Christ.
Look at Him.
Look at the cross.
Look at the empty tomb.
Look at the Savior who welcomed repentant sinners, confronted hypocrisy, cared for the broken, and gave His life to redeem His people.
He is not merely the subject of a religious season.
He is Lord.
He is Savior.
He is worthy of your whole life.
And His invitation is not limited to forty days.
It is for today.
Right now.
If you have been hiding, you can stop pretending before God.
If you have sinned, confess it and turn to Christ.
If you have wandered, return to Him.
If you have grown proud of your religious knowledge, ask Him to restore humility.
If you have grown cold, seek Him again in His Word and prayer.
And if you are not yet a believer, do not imagine that Christianity begins with mastering religious customs.
It begins with the good news of Jesus Christ—His death for sinners, His resurrection, and His call to repentance and faith.
You do not need a perfect religious record to come to Him.
You need the Savior.
Maybe your prayer today is simple.

"Lord Jesus, I have been more concerned about looking faithful than being faithful. Forgive my pride. Forgive my hypocrisy. Forgive the sins I have tried to hide. Teach me to trust Your grace, love Your truth, and follow You every day. Whether I observe Lent or not, let my life belong to You. Amen."
And if this message uncovered something you have been avoiding, I want to invite you to be honest.
You do not have to reveal private details publicly. God knows your circumstances, and Christian community should be a place where people are treated with compassion rather than shame.
Someone reading silently may need to hear that repentance is possible, forgiveness is real, and no sinner is beyond the saving power of Jesus.
Not to win a religious argument.
Not to embarrass someone who observes Lent differently from you.

But because there may be a friend, a relative, a struggling believer, or someone who has walked away from church who needs to encounter the Gospel rather than another fight about religious traditions.
Not because following a page makes someone a disciple.
But because the truth of God's Word deserves to be heard, examined, and lived.
There is also something important I want to share with those who have been blessed by this ministry.

Behind every Gospel-centered article, every biblical resource, and every message of encouragement is a continuing commitment to help people encounter the truth of Scripture and grow deeper in Jesus Christ.
Our desire is not simply to attract readers.
It is to help nurture disciples.
People who know the Word.
People who recognize false teaching.
People who understand grace without treating sin lightly.
People who can explain the Gospel to their children.
People who continue trusting Christ when life becomes painful.
And people who learn to love God not only with emotion, but with truth, obedience, and perseverance.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
But a genuine opportunity to participate in work that seeks to glorify Jesus Christ and serve others through His Word.
These products can serve as personal reminders of biblical truth, thoughtful gifts, or practical resources for faith-centered living.
It is the opportunity to help more people hear the Gospel and gain access to biblical encouragement and discipleship resources.
Others cannot.
Both are welcome.
That no religious ritual can replace the Savior.
That no amount of human effort can earn redemption.
That repentance is not merely an annual event.
That grace is never permission to remain in sin.
And that Jesus Christ is still transforming lives through the power of His Gospel.
So, should Christians observe Lent?
Here is the answer.

Christians may observe Lent as a voluntary season of prayer, fasting, repentance, and reflection upon Christ, provided they do so in a way that honors Scripture and does not treat the observance as necessary for salvation or as a measure of spiritual superiority.
Christians may also choose not to observe Lent, because the New Testament does not command the Church to keep this particular forty-day season.
Neither position gives us permission to judge another believer's standing before God merely on the basis of the observance.
The danger is not simply tradition.
It is tradition that replaces truth.
It is fasting that replaces repentance.
It is ritual that replaces relationship with Christ.
It is religious confidence that replaces humble dependence upon grace.
And it is the arrogance of believing that our preferred practice—or rejection of a practice—makes us righteous before God.
The cross destroys that illusion.
At Calvary, nobody could boast of having earned redemption.
The Savior was crucified for sinners.
And on the third day, He rose again.
That is our hope.
Not forty days of perfect fasting.
Not ashes.
Not religious superiority.
Not the absence of tradition.
Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
If you remember only one thing from this article, remember this:
You can give up something for Lent and still refuse to surrender to Christ.
You can refuse Lent and still refuse to surrender to Christ.
But when you truly come to Jesus in repentance and faith, you discover that salvation was never something you could achieve through religious performance.
It is God's gift of grace, received through faith in the Savior.
And a life transformed by that grace is called to follow Him—not merely for a season, but every day.
Because the deepest question has never been simply what you gave up for forty days.
It is whether you have entrusted your life to the One who gave Himself for you.
The tragedy would not be reaching Easter without observing Lent; it would be spending your life surrounded by reminders of the cross while never surrendering to the Savior who died upon it.
